Setup guide · Git2App · 1 Nov 2026

Set up Git2App so it can turn Xpenstack into store apps

The code is done. These are the accounts and settings only you can create. Do them in order, about 90 minutes in all. Everything is clicking and pasting in your web browser: no commands, no Git Bash, nothing to install. Steps marked "Claude can do this" I do as soon as you say go.

Your values

Type yours once. Every Copy button and link below uses them. The free Cloudflare addresses work fine; a domain of your own can come later.

Your API address is then .

The whole flow

WebsiteCloudflare Pages. You sign in and tap Build.

↓ sign-in

SupabaseAccounts, apps list, build history, locked signing keys

↓ every action

APICloudflare Worker

↓ reads code

GitHub AppRead-only, only the repos you pick

↓ starts builds

GitHub ActionsFresh Linux (Android) or Mac (iPhone) per build
Cloudflare R2Stores the finished APK, AAB and IPA for 30 days

ABefore you start

Once, about 5 minutes.

  1. Turn on two-step sign-in for GitHub, Cloudflare and Supabase. Whoever gets into one of them can change what Git2App builds.

    Open GitHub securityOpen Cloudflare securityOpen Supabase security

  2. Open your password manager and make a new note called "Git2App". Every secret below goes into that note first, and then into the one place named. Never into a chat, a screenshot or an email.

BCreate the GitHub App people install

About 15 minutes. This is how Git2App reads a repo, read-only.

  1. Open the new GitHub App form.

    Open New GitHub App

  2. Fill in these boxes, one Copy at a time.

    GitHub App name
    Homepage URL
    Identifying and authorizing users › Redirect URI (GitHub used to call it Callback URL)
    Allow wildcard matchingleave unticked
    Expire user authorization tokensleave ticked
    Request user authorization (OAuth) during installationtick it
    Webhook URL
    Webhook secret: make one here, save it in your note, then paste itnot made yet

  3. Scroll to Permissions › Repository permissions. Set Contents to Read-only. Leave everything else on No access (Metadata turns to Read-only by itself).

  4. Scroll past the permission lists. Under Subscribe to events tick Push (it appears once Contents is on). Under Where can this GitHub App be installed? choose Only on this account. Tap Create GitHub App.

  5. On the page that opens, copy the App ID and Client ID into your note. Tap Generate a new client secret and copy it into your note too (GitHub shows it once).

    Before any screenshot: cover every long code GitHub says you "won't be able to see again". A secret in a screenshot has to be replaced.

    GitHub now keeps secrets and keys on their own page: left menu › Credentials, with two tabs, Client secrets and Key pairs.

    Screenshot slot: the Client secrets section, with the secret covered.

  6. Left menu › Credentials › Key pairs tab › New key. A file ending in .private-key.pem downloads to your Downloads folder. Leave it there. You don't change it in any way: in section G you open it in Notepad and copy what's inside.

CCreate the Workers App (only for this repo)

About 10 minutes. It lets the API start and stop builds here, so people never give Git2App access to their own Actions.

  1. Open the form again and fill in:

    Open New GitHub App
    GitHub App name
    Homepage URLhttps://github.com/shubhamrkrock/PWA-to-app-converter
    Webhookuntick Active
    Repository permissionsActions: Read and write
    Where can it be installedOnly on this account

  2. Tap Create GitHub App. Copy its App ID into your note. Then left menu › Credentials › Key pairs › New key. A second .private-key.pem file downloads, with "workers" in its name. Leave it in Downloads too.

  3. In the left menu tap Install App › Install › Only select repositories › PWA-to-app-converter › Install. The address of the page you land on ends in a number: that is the installation id. Copy it into your note.

    Screenshot slot: the address bar ending in the installation id.

DTwo settings in this repo

About 5 minutes.

  1. Add the variable that tells builds which API they may talk to. Tap New repository variable.

    Open Actions variables
    NameG2A_API_ORIGIN
    Value (no slash at the end)

  2. Add the signing environment. Tap New environment, name it, then under Deployment branches and tags choose Selected branches and tags and add main. Add no secrets to it.

    Open Environments
    Environment nameg2a-signing

    Screenshot slot: the next page, Deployment branches and tags with the main rule.

Public repo, so read this (31 Oct): the repo is public for free build minutes. That means anyone can read build logs, and for one day download a release build's unsigned app. For your own Xpenstack that is fine: its web code is public on its website anyway. Before other people use Git2App, builds must move to a private repo (paid minutes) or another build service.

ESupabase: the accounts database

About 10 minutes. Separate from Xpenstack's project.

Claude can do this. Say "create the Supabase project" and I create it, run the three database files and check them. You then only do steps 3 and 4.

  1. Create a new project, name it git2app, and pick the region nearest you (Frankfurt for Europe). Save the database password in your note.

    Open New project

    The project ref is the code in its address, after /project/. Type it into Your values at the top.

  2. Open the SQL editor and run the three database files in order, one at a time: open each, copy all, paste, Run.

    Open SQL editor
    File 1File 2File 3

  3. Turn on the newer kind of sign-in keys: JWT Keys › Migrate or Create standby key, then Rotate keys so the ES256 key is in use. The API refuses the old shared-secret kind.

    Open JWT keys

    Screenshot slot: Current key ECC (P-256).

  4. Set where sign-in sends people back to.

    Open URL configuration
    Site URL
    Redirect URLs › Add URL

  5. Copy three values into your note: the Project URL, the anon (public) key and the service_role key. The service_role key is a full-access secret: it only ever goes into step G.

    Open API keys

FSign in with GitHub and Google

About 20 minutes. Email links work without this; skip it if you like and come back.

  1. GitHub sign-in. Create an OAuth app (a different thing from the GitHub App in B).

    Open New OAuth app
    Application nameGit2App
    Homepage URL
    Authorization callback URL

    Tap Register application, then Generate a new client secret.

  2. Paste that Client ID and secret into Supabase's GitHub provider and switch it on.

    Open Sign In providers

  3. Google sign-in. In Google Cloud, set up the consent screen (External, app name Git2App, your email), then create an OAuth client of type Web application.

    Open Google OAuth client
    Authorized JavaScript origins
    Authorized redirect URIs

    Screenshot slot: the Google client form, filled in.

  4. Paste the Google Client ID and secret into Supabase's Google provider and switch it on.

    Open Sign In providers

GThe API on Cloudflare

About 20 minutes, all in the Cloudflare website. Do this after Claude says the code is merged, because Cloudflare builds from main.

Claude already did the file part. Your addresses and app name are in the API's settings file.

  1. Make the storage for finished apps. Cloudflare › R2 Object Storage › Create bucket. Type the name, leave the rest, tap Create bucket. The first time, Cloudflare asks for a card: R2 is free up to 10 GB, and Git2App stays far below that.

    Open Create bucket
    Bucket namegit2app-artifacts

    Screenshot slot: the Create bucket form.

  2. Make the two job queues. Cloudflare › Queues › Create queue, type the first name, Create. Then once more with the second name.

    Open Queues
    First queuegit2app-dispatch
    Second queuegit2app-dispatch-dlq

    Screenshot slot: both queues in the list.

  3. Put the API online. Workers & Pages › Create › Import a repository › GitHub › PWA-to-app-converter. Fill in the boxes below, then tap Deploy.

    Open Create
    Project namegit2app-api
    Build commandnpm ci
    Deploy commandnpx wrangler deploy --config apps/api/wrangler.toml
    Path (root directory)leave empty

    When it says Success, the page shows the address. It should be . If it's different, send Claude the address you see.

    Screenshot slot: the import form, filled in.

  4. Add the secrets. Open the new git2app-api Worker › Settings › Variables and Secrets › Add. For each row below: set Type to Secret, paste the name with its Copy button, paste the value from your note, tap Deploy (or Save). Repeat for every row.

    Open the Worker's settings
    NameValue from
    SUPABASE_URL Supabase Project URL (E)
    SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY service_role key (E)
    GITHUB_APP_ID App ID (B)
    GITHUB_CLIENT_ID Client ID (B)
    GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET Client secret (B)
    GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET Webhook secret (B)
    GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY The first .pem file: see the next step
    WORKERS_APP_ID Workers App ID (C)
    WORKERS_APP_PRIVATE_KEY The "workers" .pem file: see the next step
    WORKERS_INSTALLATION_ID Installation id (C)
    STATE_SECRET Make one below
    TICKET_SECRET Make one below
    CREDENTIALS_MASTER_KEY Make one below
    State secretnot made yet
    Ticket secretnot made yet
    Master key: keep it in your note forever. Lose it and saved signing keys can't be opened.not made yet

    Screenshot slot: the Add variable form with Type set to Secret (value covered).

  5. How to copy a .pem file's inside. Open File Explorer (the yellow folder on the taskbar) › Downloads. Right-click the .private-key.pem file › Open with › Notepad (if Notepad isn't listed: Choose another app › Notepad). Press Ctrl+A to select everything, then Ctrl+C to copy. Paste it as the secret's value. It starts with -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----; copy all of it, nothing changed.

    When both keys are in Cloudflare, delete the two .pem files from Downloads and empty the Recycle Bin.

HThe website on Cloudflare Pages

About 10 minutes.

  1. Open Workers & Pages › Create › Pages › Import an existing Git repository and pick PWA-to-app-converter.

    Open Create Pages

  2. Fill in the build settings.

    Project namegit2app
    Production branchmain
    Framework presetNone
    Build commandnpm ci && npm run build:web
    Build output directoryapps/web/dist

  3. Open Environment variables and add three. None of them is a secret.

    VITE_SUPABASE_URL
    VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEYthe anon key from E
    VITE_API_ORIGIN

    Screenshot slot: the three variables.

  4. Tap Save and Deploy. When it says Success, open the site.

    Open the website

ICheck it works

  1. Sign in on the website. Go to GitHub › Connect GitHub and install your GitHub App on Xpenstack only.

  2. Go to Apps › New app › Xpenstack › branch dev › Add and check it. In a few minutes the check report shows Android and iPhone verdicts.

  3. Fill in Settings, then Build › Android › Testing on my phone. When it says Ready, download the APK on your Android phone.

  4. Something red? Copy the message and send it to me.

Mistakes we hit

  

    
What happenedFix

    
      
Checks never started; jobs showed no runner (31 Oct)Private repo had used its free minutes. Made the repo public, so builds are free

      
The iPhone test showed "skipped"It only runs when started by hand with "ios" ticked, by design

      
The GitHub App form had no "Callback URL" box (1 Nov)GitHub renamed it: paste it into Redirect URI

      
A screenshot sent in chat showed the webhook secret (1 Nov)Make a new one before creating the app; cover secret boxes before taking a screenshot

      
No "Private keys" or "Client secrets" on the General page (1 Nov)GitHub moved them: left menu › Credentials, tabs Client secrets and Key pairs

      
A screenshot showed the new client secret (1 Nov)Tap New secret again, save the new one, Delete the old one

      
The guide asked for Git Bash commands to convert keys and store secrets (1 Nov)Removed: Git2App now reads the key file as GitHub gives it, and everything is done by clicking in the Cloudflare website

      
Bare addresses in replies weren't tappableEvery link is now a button or a full link
